about.title: Santa Clara Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Santa Clara's workforce is spread across tech campuses, warehouses, construction sites near Lafayette Street, and delivery routes that run El Camino Real and the San Tomas Expressway. When someone gets hurt doing that work, the first question is usually simple: who pays for it? In California, workers' compensation normally covers medical care and part of lost wages no matter who was at fault, and it is typically the only claim you can bring against your employer. That is not always the end of the story, though. If a subcontractor, a property owner, the maker of a faulty tool, or another driver contributed to the injury, a separate third-party claim may be available. That distinction matters for anyone who drives for work here. Santa Clara recorded 367 injury collisions in 2025, with 496 people hurt, and reported crashes tend to cluster on Tuesdays between 5 and 7 p.m. We handle workplace injury claims and can help you understand which legal paths apply to your situation.

whyChoose.title: Why Santa Clara Workers Choose Us

items.title: Two Claims, Not One
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually your only remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party can be held separately responsible. We can review whether both apply to you.

items.title: Deadlines Kept Straight
items.desc: You generally have 30 days to report an injury to your employer, and a third-party injury claim carries a two-year deadline. Contacting us early keeps both clocks in view.

items.title: Protection From Pushback
items.desc: California law makes it illegal to fire or punish you for reporting a work injury. Our team works on contingency, so there is no fee unless you recover.

items.question: I was rear-ended on El Camino Real while driving a company van. Is that just workers' comp?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Because you were working, workers' compensation should cover your medical treatment and a portion of lost wages regardless of fault. The other driver, however, is a third party, so you may also have a separate injury claim against them. We can review the collision report and explain how the two interact.

items.question: How quickly do I need to tell my employer I was hurt?
items.answer: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days. Sooner is better, and putting it in writing helps avoid disputes later. If you're worried about how your employer will react, keep in mind that retaliation for reporting an injury is against the law.

items.question: Do you charge me anything for a free case review?
items.answer: No. We offer a free case review of your workplace injury claim. Our team works on contingency, meaning no fee unless there is a recovery.
